q: Which glue is cheap and cures at about 70°F and can withstand soaking in cool water?
n: Urea-formaldehyde is cheap, cures at room temperature (about 70°F) and resists cool water; resorcinol glue is the durable, waterproof one.

q: What are stone steps used for?
o: Bridging the top of door and window openings
Covering an inclined slab or capping concrete steps
Topping a masonry wall to shed water
Marking the corner where two walls meet
n: Stone steps are set over a sloping concrete slab or used to cap concrete steps. Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: How does nickel steel compare with carbon steel?
o: Harder; used for cutting edges of tools
More ductile; used for wire and nails
Weaker; used for sheet metal and lath
n: Alloy steels: nickel steel is stronger (structural members), chromium steel is hard and corrosion-resistant, manganese steel resists abrasion (digging tools), copper-bearing steel is used for sheet steel and lath.

q: What makes stainless steel stainless?
o: A zinc coating applied by hot-dipping
A high carbon content hardened by quenching
Copper that forms a protective patina
Chromium, or nickel with chromium, resists corrosion
n: Chromium (with or without nickel) forms a thin oxide film that protects the steel; galvanizing is a zinc coating instead.

q: Which board is described as hardboard made from relatively small particles?
n: Particle board is made from small wood particles; chipboard uses larger chips and is often veneered.

q: How is lumber piled for air-drying?
o: Stacked tight and flat to keep out the sun
Strip-piled at a slope on a solid foundation
Laid directly on the ground under a roof
Submerged in water tanks, then drained
n: Strips between layers let air move around every board, and the slope lets rain run off.

q: Which stone is very hard, strong, durable, and capable of taking a high polish?
n: Granite is hard, strong and durable and takes a high polish.

q: Calcareous clay contains about what proportion of calcium carbonate?
n: Calcareous clays contain about 15% calcium carbonate and burn yellowish.

q: What is an arch stone used for?
o: Spanning a door or window opening as an arch
Capping the top of a masonry wall
Forming the bottom of a window opening
Marking the external corner of a wall
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: What are building stones?
o: Cast blocks of cement and sand
Blocks or pieces of natural rock
Pressed blocks of lime and fiber
n: Building stone is natural rock quarried and shaped; concrete block, brick and fiber block are manufactured.

q: Which hardboard grade is flexible enough to be easily bent?
n: Standard hardboard can be bent; tempered hardboard is harder and stiffer.

q: Which board is made from wood, sugar cane, and asbestos fibers with a binder?
n: Insulating fiberboard is made of wood, cane or asbestos fibers with a binder.

q: What is rubble?
o: Rough fieldstone broken or roughly cut to size
Stone cut to exact size from a drawing
Thin stone slabs for walks and floors
Stone crushed to 3/8–6 in pieces for fill
n: Rubble is rough, irregular stone; dimension (cut) stone is finished to a drawing, flagstone is thin, and crushed rock is aggregate.

q: Structural lumber is generally what minimum size?
n: Structural lumber is heavy stock (about 3 in thick and 4 in wide and up) graded for loads.

q: How many board feet are in 10 pieces of 2 × 4 × 10 ft lumber?
n: Board feet = pieces × thickness (in) × width (in) × length (ft) / 12.

q: What is mechanical pulp?
o: Chips cooked in chemicals to free the cellulose
Chips softened by mild chemicals, then disk-refined
Recycled paper repulped with water and binder
Wood ground against a stone or refined from steamed chips
n: Mechanical pulp is ground wood; chemical pulp is cooked; semi-chemical pulp is both.

q: Which thicknesses are for structural load-bearing wall tile?
n: Load-bearing wall tile comes 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 in thick.

q: What is chromium steel known for?
n: Alloy steels: nickel steel is stronger (structural members), chromium steel is hard and corrosion-resistant, manganese steel resists abrasion (digging tools), copper-bearing steel is used for sheet steel and lath.

q: Mineral fiberboard uses fibers such as what?
n: Mineral fiberboard uses glass or rock wool; insulating fiberboard uses wood and cane fibers, straw board wheat straw, corkboard cork.

q: How is the moisture content of wood measured?
o: Oven-dry method or electric moisture meter
n: Weigh, oven-dry and reweigh, or read an electric moisture meter; moisture is a percentage of oven-dry weight.

q: Which building paper is printed for decorating interior walls?
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: What does ashlar work use?
n: Ashlar is squared, cut stone (broken, irregular coursed or regular coursed); rubble is rough stone.

q: What is concrete form paper made from?
o: Strong kraft or corrugated container paper
n: Kraft and container paper are formed into spiral tubes or boxes for casting round columns and voids.

q: What is sheathing paper mainly for?
o: Covering the core of gypsum board
Making the base of plastic laminates
An airtight barrier over walls and floors
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: What is notable about weathering steel?
o: Its rust layer protects it, so it needs no paint
It is zinc-coated at the mill and needs no paint
It contains chromium, so it stays bright
It is coated with bitumen before delivery
n: Weathering (Cor-Ten type) steel forms a tight oxide layer that stops further corrosion.

q: Which concrete brick comes from big, nationally known factories and is specified for government and multi-storey buildings?
n: Steam curing needs a plant, so it is made by large factories; hand-made brick is a backyard industry.

q: Which concrete brick size is used for load-bearing walls?
n: Concrete brick sizes: 4 × 8 × 16 in for non-load-bearing partitions; 6 × 8 × 16 in for load-bearing walls.

q: What is steel?
o: Iron with nearly all carbon removed
Iron with 2–4% carbon, cast in molds
An alloy of copper, zinc and iron
A malleable alloy of iron and carbon
n: Steel is iron with a controlled carbon content (graded by it); wrought iron has almost none, cast iron 2–4%.

q: Which board has a gypsum core?
n: Gypsum board has a gypsum core covered with paper.

q: Which is a common use of stainless steel in buildings?
o: Exterior wall panels and door frames
n: Stainless steel is used where appearance and corrosion resistance matter: panels, frames, kitchen work.

q: What is insulating paper meant to provide?
o: A cover for gypsum board cores
Bulk and trapped air, with strength
A fire barrier made of asbestos
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: What is flagstone?
o: Stone cut to size from a drawing
Rough fieldstone roughly cut to size
Stone set on top of a wall to shed water
Thin stone about 1/2 in and up, for walks and floors
n: Flagstone is thin, flat stone used as paving.

q: Which board is made from wood particles and a binder and is often faced with veneer?
n: Chipboard is wood chips with a binder, often faced with veneer.

q: What is cushioning paper mainly used for?
o: As an airtight barrier over sheathing
Under linoleum, carpet or slate roofing
As the base for plastic laminates
As a cover for gypsum board
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: Which material is easily worked, durable, light, and free from rust and corrosion?
n: Wood does not rust and is light and easy to work; steel rusts, stone is heavy, aluminum is harder to work on site.

q: What is pitch?
o: The condensate from distilling coal or wood
Asphalt thinned with a volatile solvent
Asphalt dispersed in water as an emulsion
The residue left from distilling tar
n: Tar is the distillate; pitch is the solid residue after tar is partly evaporated or distilled.

q: Flat grain occurs when annual rings run how to the surface?
n: Flat grain: rings roughly parallel to the face; edge grain: at right angles; angle grain: about 45°.

q: Pig iron is mainly used to make what?
n: Pig iron from the blast furnace is remelted to make cast iron, or refined into steel or wrought iron.

q: Which elements are added to make alloy steels?
n: Alloy steels: nickel steel is stronger (structural members), chromium steel is hard and corrosion-resistant, manganese steel resists abrasion (digging tools), copper-bearing steel is used for sheet steel and lath.

q: What is copper especially noted for?
o: Light weight with a silver-white luster
High compressive but low tensile strength
n: Copper conducts electricity and heat very well; aluminum is the light silver-white metal.

q: Softwoods are associated with what kind of trees?
n: Softwoods come from conifers; hardwoods from broad-leaved trees.

q: What is tar?
o: Distillate of coal, wood or peat
n: Tar is distilled from coal, wood, shale, peat or bone; pitch is its residue; asphalt comes from petroleum.

q: Which glue is satisfactory for dry locations not exposed to rain or water?
n: Casein glue is fine for dry interior locations but not for wet exposure.

q: What is manganese steel known for?
n: Alloy steels: nickel steel is stronger (structural members), chromium steel is hard and corrosion-resistant, manganese steel resists abrasion (digging tools), copper-bearing steel is used for sheet steel and lath.

q: What are building boards often faced with when used as finished wall and ceiling surfaces?
n: Paper- or vinyl-faced boards can be used as the finished surface.

q: Where are quoin stones laid?
o: On top of a wall to shed water
At the corner where two walls meet
At the bottom of window openings
As a horizontal band on a facade
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: What are stone lintels used for?
o: Forming the bottom of window openings
Bridging the top of door and window openings
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: Gypsum is chemically described as what?
n: Gypsum is hydrated calcium sulfate (CaSO₄·2H₂O).

q: What is aluminum foil used for in buildings?
n: Foil stops vapor and reflects radiant heat, so it faces insulation and roof sarking.

q: What does S4S mean?
n: S4S = surfaced (planed) four sides; S2S two sides; S1S one side; rough = as sawn.

q: Which clay has been subjected to high pressure until relatively hard?
n: Shale is clay hardened by pressure.

q: What is fireproofing paper made from?
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: Where is yard lumber commonly sold?
n: Yard lumber (1 and 2 in stock) is sold in retail yards for light construction; shop lumber goes to mills.

q: Load-bearing wall tile is used for the bearing walls of which buildings?
o: Light buildings, usually up to four stories
n: Structural clay tile carries loads in light buildings; the usual limit is four stories.

q: Structural lumber is cut from which part of the log?
n: Heartwood is denser and more decay-resistant than sapwood.

q: Which concrete brick is mostly a backyard industry?
n: Hand-made brick needs no plant; steam-cured brick comes from big factories.

q: How is laminating paper made into plastic laminate?
o: Impregnated with resin, then pressed under heat
Coated with gypsum slurry, then dried
n: Layers of resin-soaked paper are laminated under heat and pressure.

q: Why is lumber strip-piled for air-drying?
o: So the boards stay flat under their weight
So air can circulate around every piece
So rain cannot reach the lower layers
So the stack takes up less yard space
n: Stickers (strips) between layers leave gaps for airflow.

q: What is a sill in stone construction?
o: The stone at the top of an opening
The stone at the side of an opening
The stone at the bottom of a door or window opening
The stone on top of a wall
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: What is asphalt?
o: The condensate from distilling coal or wood
The residue left from distilling tar
A resin made from phenol and formaldehyde
A dark bitumen, natural or refined from petroleum
n: Asphalt is petroleum bitumen; tar and pitch come from coal, wood and similar materials.

q: How are structural clay tiles formed?
n: Hollow tiles are extruded through a die, then cut and fired.

q: What does coping do?
o: Marks the corner of two walls
Caps the wall top and sheds water
Spans the top of an opening
Hides a change in wall thickness
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: How much iron oxide do non-calcareous clays contain?
n: Their iron oxide content (2–10%) makes them burn buff, red or salmon.

q: Which plastics are made into foamboards?
n: Polystyrene and polyurethane are expanded about 40 times into rigid foam insulation.

q: Which board is made from cork granules and synthetic resin, compressed into sheets?
n: Corkboard is cork granules and resin compressed into sheets.

q: Copper-bearing steel is used mainly for what?
n: Alloy steels: nickel steel is stronger (structural members), chromium steel is hard and corrosion-resistant, manganese steel resists abrasion (digging tools), copper-bearing steel is used for sheet steel and lath.

q: Which igneous stone is made of quartz, feldspar, hornblende and mica?
n: Granite is igneous; marble is metamorphic; limestone is sedimentary; slate is metamorphic shale.

q: What does S2S mean?
n: S2S = surfaced (planed) two sides.

q: Which stone is mostly calcium carbonate and can form from hot-spring water?
n: Travertine is a limestone deposited by mineral springs.

q: Non-calcareous clays are silicate of alumina with which materials?
n: Calcareous clays contain about 15% calcium carbonate; non-calcareous clays have feldspar and iron oxide instead.

q: What are asphalt paving cements used for?
n: Paving cements bind the better (hot-mix) pavements; cutbacks are the liquid paving asphalts.

q: What leaves do hardwood trees have?
n: Hardwoods are broad-leaved (deciduous) trees; softwoods are conifers with needles.

q: How is gypsum plaster made?
n: Heating removes most of the water of crystallization; adding water later makes it set again.

q: What is rolled roofing used as?
n: Rolled roofing is heavy (45–120 lb/square) mineral-surfaced felt used as the finished roof.

q: Wrought iron is made by removing nearly all of what from pig iron?
n: Wrought iron is almost pure iron; cast iron keeps 2–4% carbon.

q: About how many times their original volume are polystyrene and polyurethane plastics expanded?
n: Polystyrene and polyurethane are expanded about 40 times their volume.

q: Liquid paving asphalts are called what?
n: Cutbacks are asphalt thinned with solvent so they can be applied liquid.

q: What walls is back-up tile for?
o: Walls faced with brick or facing tile
n: Back-up tile forms the inner wythe behind a facing of brick or facing tile.

q: What is a belt course for?
o: Shedding water from the top of the wall
Spanning the head of an opening
Architectural relief, or hiding a change in wall thickness
Tying two walls together at a corner
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: What is plastic foamboard used for?
n: Rigid foam resists moisture, so it insulates slab edges and foundations.

q: Paperboard is made in a type using paper pulp pressed into what thicknesses?
n: Pulp-type paperboard is pressed 3/16 or 1/4 in thick.

q: What does ROUGH wood finish mean?
n: Rough lumber is as sawn, not planed.

q: What is the usual height restriction for load-bearing wall tile buildings?
n: Load-bearing clay tile buildings are usually limited to four stories.

q: What makes a metal ferrous?
o: It is attracted to a magnet
n: Ferrous metals are iron-based; non-ferrous metals have little or no iron.

q: What weight range is given for roofing felts?
n: Roofing felts weigh about 3 to 20 lb per square; rolled roofing 45 to 120 lb.

q: Stone paneling uses slabs cut to what?
n: Paneling is dimension stone cut thin to size for facing walls.

q: Which rock is composed of cemented silica grains and may be gray, buff, light brown, or red?
n: Sandstone is silica grains cemented together; it may be gray, buff, brown or red.

q: How is semi-chemical pulp made?
o: Grinding wood against an abrasive stone
n: Semi-chemical pulp combines a mild cook with mechanical refining.

q: Yard lumber commonly consists of material in what thicknesses?
n: Yard lumber is 1 and 2 in stock for light construction.

q: How is chemical pulp made?
o: Wood ground against an abrasive stone
Chips cooked in chemicals to free the cellulose
n: Chemical pulp dissolves the lignin binding, leaving cellulose fibers.

q: What fibers are insulating papers made from?
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: Which hardboard type is described as less strong and durable than standard hardboard?
n: Low-density hardboard is weaker and less durable than standard hardboard.

q: How does igneous rock form?
o: From rock changed by heat and pressure
n: Igneous (granite) cools from magma; sedimentary is deposited; metamorphic is transformed.

q: Which resin glue is noted for excellent durability and water resistance despite being expensive?
n: Resorcinol-phenol-formaldehyde glue is expensive but very durable and waterproof.

q: When is rubblework called random?
o: When stones are squared to a drawing
When no horizontal or vertical courses are kept
When stones are laid in regular courses
n: Random rubble keeps no course lines; coursed rubble keeps horizontal ones.

q: What are the basic ingredients of cellular concrete block?
o: Cement, sand, gravel and water only
Silica sand, lime, cement and aluminum powder
n: Aluminum powder reacts to form gas bubbles, giving a light, insulating block.

q: What is kiln-dried lumber used for?
n: Kiln drying costs more but lowers moisture enough to limit movement in fine work.

q: Where is manganese steel especially useful?
o: Cutting edges of heavy digging tools
n: Alloy steels: nickel steel is stronger (structural members), chromium steel is hard and corrosion-resistant, manganese steel resists abrasion (digging tools), copper-bearing steel is used for sheet steel and lath.

q: Which lumber category is often left rough and may contain knots or defects?
n: Shop lumber may be rough with knots, since mills cut clear pieces from it.

q: Which non-ferrous metal is silver-white, light, malleable and conductive?
n: Aluminum is light and silver-white; copper is reddish; lead is heavy and soft.

q: What is a notable property of cellular concrete block?
o: Low cost compared with hollow block
n: Its closed air cells make it light and insulating.

q: What makes a metal non-ferrous?
o: It has little or no iron
n: Non-ferrous metals (aluminum, copper, zinc, lead) contain little or no iron.

q: Hardwoods come from which trees?
n: Hardwood and softwood name the tree type, not the actual hardness.

q: What marks a conifer?
o: Fronds at the top of a trunk
Needles, with seeds borne in cones
n: Conifers are softwoods; broad-leaved trees are hardwoods.

q: Which board is dense and rigid with a high proportion of asbestos fibers bonded with Portland cement?
n: Asbestos-cement board is dense and rigid: asbestos fiber bonded with Portland cement.

q: What is a jamb in stone construction?
o: The stone at the top of an opening
The stone at the side of a door or window opening
The stone at the bottom of an opening
The stone at the corner of two walls
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: What is the usual size of mineral fiberboard?
n: Mineral fiberboard usually comes 24 × 48 in.

q: What is glue-laminated timber?
o: Veneers glued with the grain crossed
Wood chips pressed with a binder
Layers glued with the grain parallel
n: Glulam layers run parallel (like a beam); plywood crosses the grain.

q: Which rock forms from clays and shales deposited in layers and separates into thin tough sheets?
n: Slate forms from clays and shales and splits into thin, tough sheets.

q: What type of paper is used to produce plastic laminates?
n: Laminating paper, resin-impregnated and pressed, makes plastic laminates.

q: Which stone is described as dark blue with faint green shades and formed from clay?
n: Argillite is a dark blue-green stone formed from clay.

q: What is vapor barrier paper for?
o: Adding bulk and trapped air for insulation
Stopping moisture vapor through walls, ceilings and floors
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: What is the main weakness of cast iron?
o: High compressive but low tensile strength
Low compressive but high tensile strength
n: Cast iron is brittle: strong in compression, weak in tension.

q: Which stone is an igneous rock containing the mineral serpentine?
n: Serpentine is a green stone named for the mineral serpentine.

q: What is the 4 × 8 × 16 in concrete brick used for?
n: Concrete brick sizes: 4 × 8 × 16 in for non-load-bearing partitions; 6 × 8 × 16 in for load-bearing walls.

q: How does sedimentary rock form?
o: From rock changed by heat and pressure
From materials deposited by water or on the surface
n: Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary.

q: What size range is crushed rock?
n: Crushed rock is broken stone for aggregate and fill; finer material is sand.

q: Where is stone flooring used?
n: Stone flooring is hard-wearing and weatherproof.

q: In coursed rubble work, what is maintained?
n: Coursed rubble keeps horizontal courses but not vertical ones.

q: Which is a common use of glue-laminated timber?
n: Glulam can be made in long, curved and deep sections for arches, beams, posts and truss chords.

q: What widths does rolled roofing come in?
n: Rolled roofing comes 18 or 36 in wide; roofing felt usually 36 in.

q: Which pitch is the most common?
n: Coal-tar pitch is the usual pitch in built-up roofing and waterproofing.

q: What is rotary cutting of veneer?
o: Slicing a squared log with a moving knife
Sawing thin sheets with a band saw
Turning a log on a lathe against a knife to peel a sheet
Cutting a half-log on a rotating frame
n: Rotary cutting peels one continuous sheet; slicing gives separate leaves with a matched figure.

q: Which metal is reddish, ductile and malleable, with high tensile strength?
n: Copper is the reddish metal; aluminum is silver-white.

q: Which metamorphic stone forms when limestone and dolomite are recrystallized?
n: Marble is limestone or dolomite recrystallized by heat and pressure.

q: How is the moisture content of wood expressed?
o: As a percentage of green weight
As a percentage of oven-dry weight
As a ratio to relative humidity
n: MC = (wet weight − oven-dry weight) / oven-dry weight × 100.

q: Which principal form of clay is found near the surface of the earth?
n: Surface clay lies near the surface; fire clay lies deeper and is more uniform; shale is hardened clay.

q: What is bitumen?
o: Only the residue of distilled coal tar
A mineral filler for asphalt mixes
Any coal or petroleum hydrocarbon binder
n: Bitumen covers asphalt, tar and pitch.

q: Which concrete brick size is for non-load-bearing partitions?
n: Concrete brick sizes: 4 × 8 × 16 in for non-load-bearing partitions; 6 × 8 × 16 in for load-bearing walls.

q: Why is an air-drying pile sloped?
o: So air enters from one side only
So more boards fit per pile
n: A slope lets rain drain away instead of soaking the stack.

q: How do structural clay tiles differ from brick?
o: Tiles are solid; brick is hollow
Tiles are unfired; brick is fired
Tiles are hollow; brick is solid
Tiles use shale; brick uses surface clay
n: Structural clay tile is a hollow unit; brick is sold as a solid unit.

q: Edge grain occurs when annual rings run approximately how to the face?
n: Edge grain: annual rings at about right angles to the face.

q: What color do calcareous clays burn to?
n: Calcareous clays burn yellowish because of their calcium carbonate.

q: Which wood group is common for glue-laminated timber?
n: Softwoods glue well and are light and cheap.

q: What determines whether non-calcareous clay burns buff, red, or salmon?
n: Iron oxide content decides whether non-calcareous clay burns buff, red or salmon.

q: What does S1S mean?
o: Surfacing or planing of one side
n: S1S = surfaced (planed) one side.

q: Which board is made from compressed wheat straw and processed at 350–400°F?
n: Straw board is compressed wheat straw processed at 350–400°F.

q: What is coping in stone construction?
o: Stone at the bottom of an opening
Stone cut to fit on top of a wall
Stone at the side of an opening
Stone bridging the top of an opening
n: Stone-construction terms: sill (bottom of an opening), jamb (side), lintel (top), quoin (wall corner), coping (wall top), belt course (horizontal band).

q: Which resin glue needs high curing temperature and is useful for combining timber and plywood?
n: Phenol-formaldehyde needs high curing heat and is used for exterior plywood.

q: Which lumber is for heavy, load-bearing construction?
n: Structural lumber is graded for strength; yard lumber is for light work; shop lumber goes to mills.

q: How is plywood made?
o: Thin veneers glued with the grain crossing
Layers glued with the grain parallel
n: Crossing the grain makes plywood stable both ways; parallel grain is glulam.

q: What is the standard brick size?
n: 2¼ × 3¾ × 8 in is the standard clay brick; 4 × 8 × 16 in is a concrete block.

q: What happens when lumber is pressure-treated?
o: The wood is dried quickly in a kiln
The surface is charred to seal it
Preservatives are forced into the wood under pressure
The wood is soaked in water to leach sap
n: Pressure forces preservative salts or oils deep into the wood against rot and insects.

q: Why is concrete brick steam-cured?
o: It gives the brick a uniform color
It removes the need for cement
It reaches high early strength in hours
n: Steam curing speeds hydration, so factories can ship within a day or two.

q: Partition tile is intended to be what?
n: Partition tile is non-load-bearing.

q: What should a lumber order state?
o: Species and color of the wood only
Pieces, size, board feet, kind and finish
Length and unit price of the lot only
n: Example: 6 pcs 2 × 8 × 14 ft, 112 bd ft, tanguile, S4S.

q: Which clay is found at deeper levels and generally has more uniform physical and chemical qualities?
n: Fire clay lies deeper and has more uniform qualities than surface clay.

q: Which lumber is for ordinary light construction and finishing?
n: Yard lumber is 1 and 2 in stock sold at retail yards.

q: What is trim stone?
o: Stone cut for a specific purpose
Stone left rough from the quarry
n: Trim stones (sills, copings, jambs) are cut for their position.

q: What are the three ashlar patterns?
o: Broken, irregular coursed and regular coursed
n: Ashlar is cut stone; rubble patterns are random or coursed; the bonds are brick patterns.

q: How many board feet are in one piece of 2 × 6 × 12 ft lumber?
n: Board feet = pieces × thickness (in) × width (in) × length (ft) / 12.

q: What does gypsum do in Portland cement?
n: Gypsum ground with the clinker controls flash setting.

q: How many board feet are in 6 pieces of 2 × 8 × 14 ft lumber?
n: Board feet = pieces × thickness (in) × width (in) × length (ft) / 12.

q: What is a veneer in plywood?
o: The finishing coat on the face
The edge band on the panel
n: Plywood is built from veneers glued with the grain crossing.

q: What is envelope paper used for?
o: The outer covering of materials like gypsum board
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: Which sedimentary stone may be oolitic or made of shell fragments?
n: Limestone is calcium carbonate, often from shells; sandstone is cemented silica grains.

q: What weight range is for rolled roofing?
n: Rolled roofing weighs about 45 to 120 lb per square.

q: What is hardboard made from?
n: Hardboard is wood fiber pressed dense; straw board and corkboard use other raw materials.

q: Angle grain occurs when annual rings are approximately how oriented to the face?
n: Angle grain: rings at about 45° to the face.

q: What thickness range does corkboard come in?
n: Corkboard insulation is made from compressed cork granules and resin.

q: Shop lumber is for which work?
o: Mills making sash, doors and cabinets
n: Shop lumber is cut up into millwork, so knots between cuts are acceptable.

q: What is dimension (cut) stone?
o: Stone cut or finished to a drawing
n: Dimension stone is made to set sizes; rubble is rough.

q: Which buildings usually specify steam-cured concrete brick?
n: Steam-cured brick is more uniform and stronger, so it is specified for major buildings.

q: How is tempered hardboard made?
o: Standard board laminated to thin steel
Board pressed from coarser, larger chips
Standard board impregnated with oil and resin, then baked
n: Tempering makes it harder, stronger and more water-resistant.

q: What are building papers generally used for?
o: Lining plumbing and drain pipes only
Underlay for paint and varnish only
n: Building papers: sheathing (airtight barrier), vapor barrier, insulating, cushioning (under floor coverings), envelope (covering gypsum board), laminating (plastic laminates), fireproofing (asbestos) and wallpaper.

q: How does metamorphic rock form?
o: From rock changed by heat and pressure
n: Marble (from limestone) and slate (from shale) are metamorphic.

q: Why is kiln-drying used despite its cost?
o: To add preservative to the wood
To limit wood movement in refined work
To bleach the color of the wood
n: Kiln-dried wood reaches a lower, controlled moisture content.

q: What is the basic ingredient of brick?
n: Clay brick is shaped and fired; concrete brick uses cement.

q: Which truss part is a common use of glulam?
n: Glulam can be curved, so it suits the curved top chord of a bowstring truss.

q: Roofing felts are commonly produced in rolls of what width?
n: Roofing felt usually comes in 36 in wide rolls.
